messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Aroha is a nineteen-year-old Māori woman who works as a fisherman on the Pacific coast, rising before dawn most mornings to crew a small commercial vessel with a handful of older colleagues. She came to the clinic after her partner urged her to seek help, having watched her grow increasingly distant and volatile over the preceding eight months. Her PCL-5 score of 49 places her firmly within the clinical range for PTSD, and the picture that emerged across the intake and first two sessions was one of a young woman caught inside a tightening loop she could neither name nor escape.

The event that precipitated her presentation occurred on an evening last winter when Aroha was cycling home from the harbour along a coastal path. She heard footsteps behind her — rapid, closing — and turned to see a man attacking a woman she recognised from the waterfront. The assault was brief but savage. Aroha froze. She did not call out, did not intervene, did not even move until it was over. By the time she found her voice, the man had gone. She had come to believe, with a certainty that felt like a verdict, that she should have protected that woman and had failed her entirely. That belief settled into her like ballast.

In the months that followed, the memory did not behave like an ordinary recollection. It forced itself into Aroha's mind without invitation — on the boat, between hauls, while she was gutting fish — arriving not always as an image but sometimes as a wave of guilt so complete that it had no picture attached to it, only weight. When the memory surfaced, the guilt was immediate and crushing, and it fed directly back into her conviction that she was someone who had failed when it mattered. That appraisal of herself as a person who could not be trusted to act — or, worse, who might act badly — began to extend in a new direction: she became frightened that she would lose control of her anger, that the rage she sometimes felt would break out of her and cause harm. The memory, by reinstating her sense of failure, kept that fear alive and sharpened it.

Her body had become its own source of alarm. Before she could consciously register a stimulus, her heart would be pounding, her muscles braced — and this physical reactivity, which she experienced as her body betraying her, reinforced her belief that something was fundamentally wrong with her. She had difficulty concentrating during even routine tasks on the vessel, and when a piece of equipment was slow to respond or a colleague took longer than expected to return from below deck, she assumed something terrible was unfolding. This hypervigilant monitoring of the environment kept her scanning for threat, and that scanning made it more likely that ordinary stimuli would register as dangerous — particularly the sound of footsteps behind her and, above all, the sight of a bicycle, which she now found almost unbearable. These triggers, when encountered, pulled the memory back with them, and the memory returned the guilt, and the guilt returned the self-appraisal, and the appraisal returned the fear — a circuit that completed itself rapidly and without her consent.

To manage it, Aroha had built a structure of avoidance that looked, from the outside, like dedication. She volunteered for every extra shift, arriving at the harbour before anyone else and staying late, because the physical exhaustion of work kept her thoughts from settling. She had stopped being intimate with her partner. She spent hours each evening on her phone, cycling through videos and games, not because she enjoyed them but because they held her attention just enough to prevent the memory from surfacing. What she had not anticipated was that this constant motion — the overwork, the screen time, the relentless occupation of her mind — was also preventing her from processing anything, so that each morning she returned to the same raw state. The maladaptive strategies that were meant to suppress the memory were, in practice, keeping her sensitised to every trigger, because she never reached a moment of genuine rest in which her nervous system could recalibrate. Her partner had noticed her flinch at footsteps in their hallway. She had not cycled since the night of the assault.

What finally brought her in was a morning on the boat when she snapped at a colleague over something trivial and saw fear cross his face. She had come to believe she was capable of something terrible, and in that moment it felt confirmed. What she most hopes for, she said quietly, is to stop feeling like a danger to the people around her. What she most fears is that the clinician will agree.
